consensus_summary: The blind consensus identifies Hell primarily as the final place or state of eternal divine punishment, conscious torment, and separation from God for the unrepentant wicked (with fire/Gehenna imagery), while listing lexical distinctions among Sheol/Hades/Gehenna/Tartarus, annihilationism, and universalism as secondary alternatives.
book_summary: The book identifies Hell as an ambiguous English translation label with no single scriptural referent, whose meaning must be taken from the underlying Hebrew or Greek term, and redirects via aliases to Sheol (for Sheol/Hades), Gehenna/Valley of Hinnom, or Tartarus.
consensus_core_identification: Final place/state of eternal punishment and separation from God for the wicked.
book_core_identification: Ambiguous English translation label with no single scriptural referent; sense fixed only by the underlying word (Sheol, Gehenna, Tartarus).
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats the various biblical terms as converging on (or at least compatible with) one primary postmortem-punishment referent called Hell; the book denies any such single referent and splits every occurrence by original-language term.
material_contradiction: Consensus core affirms Hell as a unified final-punishment reality; book core explicitly denies that “Hell” has any single scriptural referent at all.
rationale: Minimum cores cannot both be true of the same term in the same sense: one asserts a determinate eschatological place/state, the other asserts the absence of any single referent and replaces the English word with distinct original terms. The lexical-distinction view appears among consensus alternatives, yet the book elevates it to the sole identification and thereby rejects the consensus primary. This is replacement of the central referent, not a mere boundary adjustment around the same category.
strongest_objection: Traditional theology already knows the underlying terms differ yet still synthesizes them into one coherent doctrine of final punishment; the book’s ‘no single referent’ claim therefore overstates translational ambiguity into ontological denial.
